analysis.one_liner: Lifts all limits on campaign contributions and ends public financing of presidential campaigns, while tightening disclosure.
analysis.headline: This campaign-finance bill, backed by 71 cosponsors, was reported out of committee in August 1999 but never received a House floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it legal, starting in 2001, for anyone to give unlimited money to federal candidates and parties, and would have ended the taxpayer checkoff that publicly funds presidential campaigns. In exchange, it tightened disclosure: parties would have to report soft money transfers to the FEC, all committees would file electronically, reports would appear online within 24 hours, and large late contributions would have to be disclosed within a day.
analysis.who_benefits: Wealthy individuals and big donors, who after 2000 could give unlimited amounts directly to candidates and parties; national and state party committees, which could raise unlimited money and route it through state parties; and candidates with access to large donors. Disclosure rules would also help journalists and voters see where the money came from.

how_it_helps.text: Parties would have to report to the FEC all funds transferred to state and local party committees, even money not counted as contributions under existing law (soft money).
All political committees would have to file reports electronically, and the FEC would have to post report information on the Internet within 24 hours of receiving it.
Contributions received in the final 90 days before an election would have to be reported within 24 hours, covering every campaign committee, not just the principal committee.
Committees could no longer use the 'best efforts' exception to avoid penalty for failing to identify contributors who give more than $200 in a year.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary voters would lose relative influence: unlimited contributions would let a single large donor match the power of thousands of small ones, and the voluntary taxpayer checkoff that publicly funds presidential campaigns would end, leaving presidential candidates fully dependent on private money.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes every federal contribution limit for contributions made after 2000, so a single wealthy donor could legally give unlimited sums to a candidate or party committee.

It terminates the income tax checkoff for the Presidential Election Campaign Fund after 1999 and shuts down the Fund and the primary matching payment account after 2000, ending public financing of presidential campaigns.

By pairing unlimited contributions with disclosure but no limits, the bill would leave large donors free to fund candidates as long as the money was reported, which was the core objection of campaign-finance reformers at the time.
The strict reporting rules (24-hour notifications and no 'best efforts' defense) would impose real compliance burdens on campaign treasurers, especially for small campaigns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The disclosure improvements are genuine and would have made campaign money visible to voters far faster. But they are paired with the bill's central change: eliminating all contribution limits. In practice, transparency about unlimited money is a weaker protection than limits on it, because it lets donors give as much as they want and simply tells voters afterward. Ending presidential public financing compounds the shift toward privately funded campaigns.

outcome.mechanism: The House Administration Committee reported the bill in August 1999 and it was placed on the Union Calendar, but House leaders never scheduled a floor vote and it died when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 25, 1999 by Rep. John Doolittle, with Rep. Tom DeLay and 71 cosponsors (69 Republicans and 2 Democrats).
On August 2, 1999 the Committee on House Administration considered and marked up the bill, ordering it reported without recommendation by voice vote; it was reported on August 5.
The Ways and Means Committee was discharged from the bill on August 5, 1999, and it was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 176.
No further action was taken: the bill never received a House floor vote, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, existing federal contribution limits and the taxpayer checkoff for presidential campaigns stayed in place, and large donors did not gain the right to unlimited giving during this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing contribution limits stayed in place

for.role: Committee with jurisdiction over campaign finance reporting
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill on August 2, 1999 and reported it without recommendation by voice vote on August 5, 1999 (H. Rept. 106-296).

against.role: Majority leadership controlling the House floor schedule
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a House floor vote after it was placed on the Union Calendar in August 1999; it sat there until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 69 of the 71 cosponsors were House Republicans, with only 2 Democrats, and the bill was reported from committee by voice vote without recommendation.

industries.industry: Large individual donors and wealthy households
industries.note: The bill would have allowed unlimited contributions to federal candidates and parties after 2000, letting a single large donor's money rival the combined voice of many small donors. Disclosure would reveal the gifts but not cap them.

Parties could raise unlimited money and route it through state and local committees, with the bill making those transfers the disclosed, lawful channel for large sums. The disclosure requirement adds transparency but also legitimizes the pipeline.

Removing all contribution limits would have increased the total money in federal campaigns, most of which is spent through consultants and media buys. More fundraising means more paid advertising volume.
